editorNote: Commodore has bought itself a startling new future: Amiga’s color-rich Lorraine project now sits at the center of the home-computer contest.
morningLine: Amiga changes hands, the PC/AT flexes its muscle, and adventurous games redraw the home-computer map.

lead.headline: Commodore Bets on Amiga's High-Tech Macintosh Rival
lead.dek: The rescued Lorraine project promises vivid color, 32-bit ambition, and a fresh answer to Apple and Atari.
body: Commodore International has agreed to acquire privately held Amiga Corporation, bringing one of the personal-computer industry’s most closely watched experimental machines under the company that made the VIC-20 and Commodore 64. Terms were not disclosed, but the purchase gives Commodore a dramatic new technology platform just as competition in home computing is being rearranged.

Amiga had demonstrated a Macintosh-like computer expected to sell for about $1,500, well below the Macintosh’s $2,495 price. Period reports emphasized its advanced processor class and unusually capable color graphics—features that could move a friendly graphical computer out of the monochrome office and into games, animation, and the living room.

The deal also sharpens a personal rivalry. Former Commodore president Jack Tramiel now controls Atari’s consumer operations, while Commodore chief Marshall Smith has promised a small, high-performance Macintosh-like machine for “well under $1,000.” Amiga’s engineering gives that promise more weight, even if the final product and price remain unsettled.

For Amiga, Commodore’s backing may be the difference between an impressive demonstration and a computer that reaches store shelves. For Commodore, the gamble is whether it can turn sophisticated custom chips and a daring design into a reliable, affordable family of machines before Apple, IBM, and the revived Atari seize the next generation.

stories.headline: IBM's PC/AT Launch Echoes Through the Week
body: IBM’s model 5170 Personal Computer AT continues to reset expectations across the business-computer market. Built around Intel’s 80286, IBM says the machine runs more than twice as fast as existing members of its PC family and offers eight expansion slots, six ready for new 16-bit cards.

The entry configuration carries 256K of memory and a 1.2-megabyte floppy drive; the larger model combines 512K with a 20-megabyte fixed disk. DOS 3.0 supports both new storage formats while retaining read compatibility with older PC-family disks.

The specifications make the AT more than a speed bump. Its memory range, expansion bus, and storage capacity establish a new target for software houses and compatible-machine builders—one that will reverberate long after this launch season.

stories.headline: Home-Computer Games Move Beyond the Arcade Formula
body: The newest computer games are asking players to explore, plan, and improvise instead of merely chasing a high score. Dan Bunten’s Seven Cities of Gold creates a new map for each expedition and mixes discovery, trade, and conflict across a broad simulated world.

First Star’s Boulder Dash turns the underground into a quick-thinking puzzle, with gems to collect, caves to dig, and rocks whose weight can help or crush the player. Heist and Super Pipeline add still more variety to the August review shelf.

Infocom’s Cutthroats, released earlier this month, carries the trend into prose. Its treasure-diving mystery relies on conversation, navigation, and careful choices—a reminder that the home computer is becoming its own game medium rather than a small imitation of the arcade.

stories.headline: Macintosh and PCjr Face the Review Bench
body: BYTE’s August review bench places two of 1984’s most discussed machines under sustained examination: Apple’s Macintosh and IBM’s PCjr. Their contrasting designs make the issue a useful buyer’s snapshot of graphical ambition on one side and PC-family compatibility on the other.

The magazine also tests Sanyo’s MBC-550, the Juki 6100 printer, and four Logo implementations for the IBM PC. Technical features on Framework, the 65816 processor, FORTH-83, and UNIX benchmarking show how quickly the conversation is widening beyond simple hardware comparisons.

bbsNote.headline: A $129 Apple modem puts The Source one slot away
bbsNote.summary: August's COMPUTE! reported two concrete steps toward easier consumer telecomputing: ZOOM's inexpensive bundled modem and STC's Apple Sourcelink automation software.

posts.text: ZOOM's $129 single-slot package combined a direct-connect 300-baud modem, terminal software, and a free Source subscription; the $179 configuration added Netmaster.

posts.platform: Apple II family; Telenet, Uninet, Sourcenet and The Source
posts.text: Sourcelink automated dialing and sign-on, offered one-button service access, captured online text to memory or disk, and transferred files while online.

curiosity.headline: Your new modem came with an online-service subscription
curiosity.summary: ZOOM used access to The Source as part of the hardware bundle, foreshadowing the service-packaging tactics of later online eras.
curiosity.detail: For $129, an Apple owner received the 300-baud Networker modem, terminal software, and a free subscription to The Source; the enhanced Netmaster bundle cost $179.
